what_it_does: When a new GPU chip is designed, engineers and cloud providers need to know how fast it will run real AI workloads before they build it or buy it in bulk — but actually running experiments on hardware that does not yet exist is impossible. Prior machine-learning-based prediction tools treat the whole AI operation (say, a matrix multiply) as a black box and try to predict its total time directly, which breaks badly when the GPU or the AI model is unfamiliar. NeuSight instead breaks each operation into the small tiles (chunks of work) that a GPU naturally processes one streaming processor at a time, predicts the time for each tile, and adds them up. It also anchors its predictions to the roofline model — a well-understood physical limit based on a chip's peak math speed versus its memory bandwidth — so the learned model cannot stray into physically impossible territory.
